  • RAS proteins are associated with small G proteins.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child presents with multiple freckle-like dark spots on sun-exposed areas such as the face and arms. The child complains of discomfort and pain upon exposure to sunlight, and there is evidence of sunburn even after brief periods outdoors. Upon further questioning, they reveal a family history of skin cancer in relatives who also experienced similar skin issues from a young age. What is the most likely diagnosis and the genetic defect in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
de excision repair

Explanation: 

This presentation is suggestive of Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), a condition caused by defective nucleotide excision repair of DNA, leading to extreme sun sensitivity, freckling, and a family history of early-onset skin cancer​​​​​​.

  • An autosomal recessive disorder characterized by sun sensitivity, with approximately 50% of patients having acute burning on minimal sun exposure.
  • UV radiation causes the cross-linking of pyrimidine residues, preventing normal DNA replication. Nucleotide excision repair (NER) prevents this DNA damage.
  • Inherited loss-of-function mutations in any of these genes give rise to xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • The onset of freckling (lentigines) on sun-exposed skin before age two years in most patients.
  • At an early age, there is a significantly increased risk of sunlight-induced cutaneous neoplasms (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma).

Xeroderma pigmentosum, defective homologous repair (Option A): It is not caused by defective homologous repair.

Cockayne syndrome, nucleotide excision repair (Option B): It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective nucleotide excision repair, but unlike XP, it doesn't increase cancer risk. It is classified as a progeroid (premature aging) syndrome.

Bloom syndrome, defective homologous repair (Option D): It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in a helicase required for homologous recombination repair.



Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page no. 314 Fitzpatrick’s Dermatology, 9th edition, Page no. 2343, 2347

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is associated with a defect in homologous DNA repair?
questions.solutionHtml:
g>Fanconi Anaemia is associated with a defect in homologous DNA repair.
  • An autosomal recessive disorder due to failure to repair ds DNA breaks (caused by UV lights) due to defective homologous repair (due to mutation in multiple genes).
  • Characterised by:
    • Developmental abnormalities (short stature, skeletal abnormalities).
    • Hypersensitivity to chemotherapeutic agents that cross-link DNA.
    • Increased risk of bone marrow failure (aplasia) and leukaemia.
  • Other diseases associated with a defect in homologous DNA repair:
    • Bloom syndrome.
    • Ataxia telangiectasia.
    • Familial breast cancer (mutations in BRCA 1 and BRCA 2).
    • Werner syndrome.
    • Rothmund-Thomson syndrome.

Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) (Option A) is a rare autosomal recessive multisystem disorder characterised by defect in the TC-NER pathway (Transcription coupled-nucleotide excision repair pathway).

Endometrial carcinoma (Option C): Certain subsets of endometrial cancer (most often) and colon cancer harbour mutations in DNA polymerase that result in a loss of proofreading function and the accumulation of numerous point substitutions.

Wermer syndrome (Option D): Wermer syndrome, also known as multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 (MEN 1) is characterised by tumors of the Parathyroid (adenoma), Pancreas (M/C- gastrinoma), and Pituitary adenoma (M/C- prolactinoma).

 



Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page no. 314,315 Fitzpatrick’s Dermatology, 9th edition, Page no. 2345

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true regarding Lynch syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: It is autosomal recessive in inheritance.

options.label: B
options.text: It is also known as hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.

options.label: C
options.text: It is caused by mutations in genes involved in nonhomologous end-joining repair.

options.label: D
options.text: Amsterdam II criteria are used for diagnosis.

questions.answerText: Amsterdam II criteria are used for diagnosis.
questions.solutionHtml:
e given options, the Amsterdam II criteria are used to diagnose Lynch syndrome (also called Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer or HNPCC).

  • An autosomal dominant disorder (Option A ruled out)

  • Caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM. (Option c ruled out)

  • Amsterdam II criteria and Revised Bethesda guidelines are clinical tools used for screening and diagnosing Lynch syndrome. (Option D)

 

Feature Description
Inheritance Autosomal dominant
Also known as Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC)
Caused by Mutations in MMR genes (not NHEJ genes)
Diagnostic criteria Amsterdam II criteria, Bethesda criteria
Associated cancers Colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urinary tract

 

It is also known as hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (Option B): Incorrect – that refers to BRCA1/2 mutations, not Lynch syndrome.

 



Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page no. 314 SRB Manual of Surgery, 6th edition, Page no. 892

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the Warburg effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Cancer cells primarily rely on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production.

options.label: B
options.text: It involves a shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells.

options.label: C
options.text: Cancer cells exhibit increased glucose uptake and preferentially metabolise glucose via glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen.

options.label: D
options.text: It is characterised by decreased glucose uptake and utilisation by cancer cells.

questions.answerText: Cancer cells exhibit increased glucose uptake and preferentially metabolise glucose via glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen.
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>

The Warburg Effect, a distinctive metabolic feature of cancer cells, involves increased glucose uptake and a preference for glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation, even in the presence of oxygen.

  • Otto Warburg was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1931 for this theory.
  • Even in the presence of ample oxygen, cancer cells demonstrate a distinctive form of cellular metabolism characterised by high glucose uptake levels and increased glucose conversion to lactose (fermentation) via glycolysis (Option D ruled out)
  • Even though ATP production is low with lactate formation compared to mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, it provides metabolic intermediates needed for synthesising cellular components.
  • Application: Positive emission tomography (PET).
    • Patients are injected with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a non-metabolizable glucose derivative preferentially taken up into tumour cells (due to glucose hunger), which can be detected by PET scan.

 

Cancer cells primarily rely on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production (Option A), which is not true, as cancer cells prefer glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen.

It involves a shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells (Option B), which is incorrect because the Warburg effect involves the opposite: a shift toward glycolysis.

 



Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th edition, Page no. 299,300

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms is not employed by tumour cells to evade the host immune system?

options.label: A
options.text: Selective outgrowth of the antigen-negative variants

options.label: D
options.text: Enhanced antigen presentation to promote T cell activation

questions.answerText: Enhanced antigen presentation to promote T cell activation
questions.solutionHtml:
Meta" data-dictid="782b31281a1692777181708484c1d1">antigen presentation is not a mechanism tumour cells employ to evade the host immune system.
  • Antigen presentation is a crucial step in activating T cells and initiating an immune response against tumour cells.
  • Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells) present tumour antigens to T cells via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, leading to T cell activation and anti-tumour immune responses.
  • While tumour cells may downregulate or alter the expression of MHC molecules to evade immune recognition, enhancing antigen presentation to promote T-cell activation is not a typical strategy employed by tumour cells for immune evasion.
  • Mechanisms by which tumour cells evade the host immune system:
    • Selective outgrowth of the antigen-negative variants (Option A ruled out).
    • Reduced expression of MHC molecules (Option Bruled out).
    • Secretion of immunosuppressive factors (Option C ruled out).
    • Engagement of pathways that inhibit T-cell activation.
      • Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been developed that inhibit CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1.
      • These can be used in the treatment of malignancies such as melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, head and neck cancers, and lymphomas
